back: Waxing slope (convex), free face (cliff), constant slope (straight) and waning slope (concave).
Creep on convex upper slopes; falls on free faces; mass movement and wash on straight slopes; wash and deposition on concave lower slopes.

The whole slope becomes gentler as time passes; the maximum angle falls.
Slopes keep the same angle as they retreat; a pediment grows at the foot (pediplanation).
A gentler lower slope grows at the expense of a steeper upper slope.
Scarp retreat and the growth of pediments until they join to form a pediplain, leaving residual inselbergs.
Deep chemical weathering in the humid tropics followed by stripping of the regolith, which exposes the weathering front as an etchplain.
The lowest level to which a river can erode (normally sea level); a fall makes rivers cut down and steepens slopes.
